transcript.text: Thank you, Elena. Here is my final recommendation on each open item. On voluntary disclosure: I recommend yes — we should make a voluntary disclosure to DOJ. Given that we have a confirmed, quantified improper-payment figure and a narrowly defined subpoena scope, proactive disclosure is the right employment-law posture and aligns with our obligations to preserve a cooperative relationship with the government. On repayment amount: I concur with Maya's recommendation of $275,000 as the proposed repayment figure, with a notation that it is preliminary pending completion of the investigation. From an employment-law standpoint, I would add that the response packet should note the repayment proposal does not constitute an admission of individual liability for any employee, including the implicated vice president. On investigation scope: I defer to Thomas on the subpoena-scope specifics of the four distributors and the 2019–2021 period, but I recommend the investigation plan include an employment-law review of personnel actions and supervisory authority related to the commission payments at issue. On the executive-interview protocol: as I confirmed this morning, the implicated vice president has retained separate counsel and will not participate in a company interview without that counsel's written consent. I recommend we adopt a formal protocol requiring written consent from the VP's separate counsel before any company interview proceeds, that we document this constraint in the response packet so DOJ understands the limitation, and that we include a fallback provision — if the VP's counsel declines or conditions participation unreasonably, we note that we will rely on documentary evidence and other witness interviews rather than compelled participation. I also recommend the protocol make clear that the company is not waiving any privileges or employment-law protections by acknowledging this constraint. Those are my final recommendations on all open items.
